outcomes: Distinguish population claims, sample estimates and independent sampling units
Implement and interpret a whole-machine percentile bootstrap interval
Compute counted calibration bins and distinguish probability error from decision accuracy
lessons: What can eighteen readings tell us?

population.name: Population
population.definition: The complete set of cases addressed by an inference.
population.explanation: A population is defined by the claim, not merely by a stored file. It might be future devices of one type, patients meeting criteria, or requests arriving after deployment. An evaluation sample supports that population only when its selection and measurement process are relevant. A precise confidence interval around a biased or mismatched sample does not repair the mismatch. State the target population whenever reporting a metric.

sample.name: Sample
sample.definition: A finite set of observed cases drawn from a population.
sample.explanation: Models are evaluated on samples because the full population is usually unavailable. A sample statistic changes when the sampled cases change. Independence, grouping, time, and selection affect how much information the sample provides. Repeated rows from one entity should not automatically be counted as independent evidence about new entities. Record selection rules and sample size alongside every reported estimate. Samples need provenance.

statistic.name: Statistic
statistic.definition: A numerical summary computed from observed sample data.
statistic.explanation: Accuracy and Brier score are statistics when computed from held-out predictions and observed outcomes. They do not reuse the scalar loss recorded while fitting the model. Their values exactly describe the evaluation sample but are uncertain estimates of population performance. Bootstrap resampling approximates how one named statistic varies, so every replicate must recompute that same statistic. Different metrics generally have different sampling distributions and intervals.

bootstrap.name: Bootstrap
bootstrap.definition: A resampling method that repeatedly draws observations with replacement.
bootstrap.explanation: A replicate draws the original number of declared sampling units with replacement and recomputes the statistic. Whole-machine draws retain complete paired sequences; unequal group sizes can produce different replicate row counts. The empirical distribution describes sampling variability under the assumed unit independence. More repetitions reduce simulation noise, not sampling bias or drift. Tiny samples still have fragile interval coverage.

calibration.name: Calibration
calibration.definition: Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcome frequencies.
calibration.explanation: If positive-class probabilities near 0.8 are calibrated for a target population, about 80 percent of comparable cases should have a positive outcome. Reliability diagrams estimate calibration by grouping predictions, then comparing each bin's mean predicted probability with its observed positive-outcome frequency. Results depend on bins and sample size. Calibration differs from ranking ability and can change when the deployment population changes. A fitted calibrator needs predictions independent of base-model fitting.

brier-score.name: Brier score
brier-score.definition: Mean squared error between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes.
brier-score.explanation: For each evaluation row, subtract its zero-or-one observed outcome from its predicted probability, square, then average over rows. Lower is better. The score penalizes confident mistakes more than cautious ones and uses information accuracy discards. It combines calibration, resolution, and outcome uncertainty, so a lower Brier score by itself is not proof of better calibration. Compare it on the same held-out cases and report the sample size.
